children: 2128 ET - The global investment community appears likely to circle the wagons over coming weeks as risk factors escalate. Technology stocks are set to report profits, and any misstep could trigger shock waves, ANZ says in a note to clients. Energy prices also remain elevated as tensions in the Middle East escalate, maintaining pressure on central banks to hike. Sovereign debt concerns have resurfaced amid riots across France, it adds. Meanwhile U.S. fiscal metrics continue to deteriorate, with net interest payments exceeding 1 trillion U.S. dollars per year. The U.S. midterm elections are likely to increase the risk of policy deadlock, it adds. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1751 ET - Despite a challenging housing market, Home Depot is benefiting from innovations and a scale that few competitors can match, Morgan Stanley analysts write in a note. "The combination of scale, cash generation and continuous reinvestment creates a competitive advantage that is difficult for smaller players to replicate," they write. The company continues to effectively leverage technology and AI, and is leveraging its physical scale to boost same- and next-day delivery, the anaylsts say. "Individually, these initiatives may appear incremental, but collectively they strengthen HD's customer proposition," they write. "We see few competitors with the scale or investment capacity to match HD's pace of innovation." (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1748 ET - Home Depot is executing well and gaining market share against a difficult macroeconomic backdrop, Morgan Stanley analysts write in a note. Consumers are putting off large projects or debt-financed renovations, with weak visibility toward an improvement in the macro picture. Still, Home Depot has defended its profitability and margins while targeting share gains and growth in the estimated $700 billion addressable Pro market. "The focus is on controllable initiatives rather than relying on a macro recovery," the analysts write. "An eventual normalization in housing activity represents upside to the thesis, rather than a prerequisite for operational progress." (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1444 ET - AI agents could start monetizing the traffic they direct to travel booking platforms in the long term, Deutsche Bank analysts say in a note. If that happens, AI agents wouldn't be a substitute for online travel platforms like Expedia and Booking, as some investors have worried, the analysts say. Instead, agents would be "more like another performance marketing channel," they say. Additionally, travel platforms have important leverage, given they could choose to restrict bot access to inventory, pricing or booking functionality, they say. The platforms' loyalty programs and direct traffic are still key, too, they say. "Net-net, we continue to view AI as a structural watch item rather than an immediate estimate driver," they say. (kelly.cloonan@wsj.com)

1439 ET - Investors continue to raise concerns over how AI agents will affect the businesses of online travel companies like Booking and Expedia, Deutsche Bank analysts say in a note. The key question is whether agents will be a new intermediary between consumers and travel suppliers, or if they'll simply be another channel for the companies to acquire customers, they say. The analysts see the latter as the most likely outcome in the near term, with agents directing customers intent on booking travel toward scaled platforms. For now, AI referral traffic remains de minimis relative to total traffic, but it continues to grow and warrants monitoring, the analysts say. (kelly.cloonan@wsj.com)

1433 ET - Ahead of quarterly results from companies like Airbnb, Booking and Expedia, travel demand data paints a mixed picture, Deutsche Bank analysts say in a note. Fewer people flew in the third quarter from a year ago, and several digital engagement datasets point to weaker trends since second quarter earnings, the analysts say. A recent survey also shows U.S. monetary concerns remain elevated, they add. On the flipside, hotels' revenue per available room trends have improved, and travelers are showing more interest than ever in alternative accommodations, among other promising signals, they say. All in, those data points "continue to point to a mixed but generally healthy travel backdrop, with higher oil prices, elevated fares and heightened monetary concerns weighing on affordability and travel intent," they say. (kelly.cloonan@wsj.com)

1400 ET - Consumer spending at restaurants and bars was up 8% year-over-year in September, UBS analysts say in a note, citing government data. The increase marks a sequential acceleration from August and outpaces retail spending growth, which was up 6.8% in September. Restaurant spending as a share of consumers' wallet ticked up slightly, though spending as a share of stomach edged lower, as consumers favored spending at grocery stores, the analysts say. "We anticipate underlying restaurant demand and share of wallet trends should be largely consistent through the balance of '26, driven by value efforts, marketing, menu innovation, and other initiatives, despite a still pressured macro environment," they say. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

1358 ET - Health across the restaurant sector appears mixed heading into 3Q results, UBS analysts say in a research note, citing uneven takeaways across consumer sentiment results, industry data, industry conversations and early financial commentary. "Our view is that while challenged, the industry may be healthier than some of the consumer sentiment and other sales data suggest," the analysts say. They note valuations across the restaurant sector appear attractive relative to history, with investors last week backing out of AI stocks and rotating into restaurant and other consumer stocks instead. Still, the analysts add, "outperformers appear increasingly concentrated among select brands in the current environment."(connor.hart@wsj.com)

1253 ET - Tokenized gold, or trading of gold using blockchain systems, is growing quickly, says the World Gold Council in a note. But it's still only a sliver of the $13 trillion market capitalization of the physical gold market worldwide, says the WGC. "Tokenised gold generated $90 billion of cumulative spot trading volumes in the first quarter of 2026, more than in the whole of 2025," says the WGC. The agency says that there's ample room for the tokenized commodity to grow, unlocking roughly $700B in what the WGC calls 'latent demand.' This demand would come from users of crypto platforms that don't currently have exposure to gold, says the agency. Most-active gold futures are down 0.5% to $4,162 per troy ounce at midday. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com)

1208 ET - Canadian railroads will need to find a new growth driver to replace grain, posing a particular challenge to Canadian National Railway, Raymond James analysts write in a note, downgrading the stock to market perform. "Grain-the dominant growth engine for both carriers through 2026-should remain healthy in absolute terms, but fade rapidly in terms of outsized growth contribution, increasing the importance of replacement growth surfacing elsewhere," the analysts write. While Canadian Pacific Kansas City has solid growth prospects outside of grain, CN Rail has "fewer obvious replacement growth drivers," they write. "The handoff therefore appears more challenging at CN." Shares fall 1.9% to $119.45. (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1152 ET - Coinbase is set to showcase how its diversification efforts are accelerating when it reports 3Q results next week, StoneX analyst Mark Palmer says in a note. Investors will likely — and wrongly — still be looking to see how much retail traders paid the exchange to trade crypto this past quarter, Palmer says. But the company has rebuilt its revenue base around derivatives, stablecoins, lending, payments and software agents that transact on their own, he says. The market has yet to price in the fact that Coinbase is becoming a full-fledged financial account for both people and the AI agents that are acting on their behalf, the analyst says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1147 ET - Even as businesses increasingly report generating value from AI, they have some work to do to mitigate AI risks, according to research firm Gartner. CIOs and ITs heads surveyed by the firm say that AI risk in their organizations is growing faster than AI value, even as 58% of functional leaders in a 2Q survey said that they saw positive value from AI initiatives. Gartner says this increases the pressure to align technology and business risk, something only 25% of CIOs currently do, according to a survey in 3Q. "The new CIO imperative is to align value with risk and align safety with governance," Gartner analyst Daryl Plummer says. "Alignment is the key." (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)
